a: Ignatius, also called Theophorus
p: Every letter opens with the same second name: Theophorus, 'God-bearer'.
b: Greek Theophoros, 'God-bearer'. Lake's footnote to the first letter gives the story of the third-century Acts of Ignatius: asked who Theophorus is, Ignatius answers, 'He who has Christ in his heart.' See the note at Ignatius to the Romans 1:0.

a: to her who has been blessed
p: The Greek names no noun here; 'her' is the church, as Lake's footnote says.
b: Greek tē eulogēmenē, 'to the (woman) who has been blessed'. The participle is feminine and has no noun with it. Lake's footnote: 'i.e. the Church'. The greeting then names her: 'the church that is in Magnesia'. Ignatius to the Romans 1:0 and Ignatius to the Trallians 1:0 also pile up words of praise around the feminine word ekklēsia, 'church'.

a: Magnesia on the Maeander
p: A city a day's walk from Ephesus, named for the great river of its valley.
b: Lightfoot describes the city: it stood not on the Maeander itself but on a tributary, the Lethaeus, some four miles from the larger river, and was called 'on the Maeander' to tell it apart from another Magnesia, 'under Sipylus'. It commanded the pass on the road between the Maeander valley and Ephesus, which Pliny puts 15 Roman miles away, and its great temple was that of Artemis Leucophryene. Because the two cities were so near, Lightfoot thought the Magnesian church was probably founded during Paul's years in Ephesus, when 'everyone living in Asia heard the Lord's word' (Acts 19:10).

a: a name most fit for God
p: Ignatius does not say which name he has been counted worthy of.
b: Greek onomatos theoprepestatou. Lake: 'a most godly name'. The letter does not say what the name is. Two of its own lines are close at hand: it is right 'not only to be called Christians, but to be Christians' (4:1), and 'Whoever is called by any name other than this does not belong to God' (10:1). His second name, Theophorus, 'God-bearer', is another possibility (1:0). The chains he carries are what earned it: the same Greek word is used of 'chains most fit for God' in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:1.

a: a union of the flesh and spirit of Jesus Christ
p: Union (henōsis) is Ignatius's watchword: of flesh and spirit, faith and love, Jesus and the Father.
b: Greek henōsis, 'union', kept apart from henotēs, 'unity' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:2). Ignatius prays for three unions in the churches: of Christ's flesh and spirit (against those who made his flesh unreal, 9:1; 11:1), of faith and love, and of Jesus and the Father. The same three return at the end of the letter: 'so that there may be a union both of the flesh and of the spirit' (13:2). Paul's 'one body and one Spirit' (Ephesians 4:4) is near in thought.
orig: ἕνωσιν ... σαρκὸς καὶ πνεύματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ

a: the ruler of this age
p: Ignatius's name for the devil, from Paul's 'rulers of this age'.
b: Greek ho archōn tou aiōnos toutou, as in Ignatius to the Ephesians 17:1 and 19:1 and Ignatius to the Romans 7:1. Paul speaks of 'the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing' (1 Corinthians 2:6), and John of 'this world's ruler' (John 12:31). For Ignatius the abuse that comes on believers, his own chains included, is the devil's work, to be endured and escaped.

a: we will reach God
p: Ignatius's phrase for the end of his journey: to die as a martyr and so come to God.
b: Greek theou teuxometha, from tynchanō, 'reach, gain'; elsewhere Ignatius uses the compound epitynchanō (14:1), and the site renders both 'reach God'. Lake: 'attain unto God'. Here the 'we' takes in the Magnesians: every believer who endures will reach God. On Ignatius's own hope of reaching God through death, see the note at Ignatius to the Romans 1:1.

a: So I was counted worthy to see you
p: The Greek sentence that begins here never ends; Ignatius takes it up again in 6:1.
b: The verse begins 'Since then I was counted worthy to see you ...' and breaks off. Lake's English footnote: 'The sentence is unfinished: possibly the text is corrupt.' Lightfoot reads it as a long-suspended sentence: the 'since' of 2:1 is 'resumed' in 6:1 ('Since then in the persons mentioned above ...') and 'at length matched' by 'I urge you' there. The Plain English Translation makes 2:1 a whole sentence and lets 6:1 pick up the thought.

a: Damas, your overseer
p: Magnesia sent its overseer, two elders and a deacon to meet the prisoner at Smyrna.
b: Damas the overseer (episkopos), the elders (presbyteroi) Bassus and Apollonius, and the deacon (diakonos) Zotion: Lightfoot notes that the Magnesian delegation 'comprised all orders of the ministry', and that the letter was written 'in acknowledgement of the attention' the church had shown him. In The Christian Ministry (page 50), writing of the overseers the letters name, Damas among them, he adds: 'Under any circumstances it seems probable that these were not fictitious personages, for, even if he were a forger, he would be anxious to give an air of reality to his writings'. Nothing more is known of any of the four.

a: my fellow slave the deacon Zotion
p: Ignatius calls the deacons his fellow slaves, as in his other letters.
b: Greek syndoulos, 'fellow slave', as the site's Revelation 6:11 and Colossians 1:7 use the word of Christ's servants. Ignatius uses it of deacons in Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:1 (Burrhus) and Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:2. 'Deacon' (diakonos) is the office, as in Philippians 1:1, 'with overseers and deacons'.

a: May I have the benefit of him
p: The verb is the one Paul uses in his play on the name Onesimus.
b: Greek onaimēn, from oninēmi. Paul writes 'let me gain something from you in the Lord' (Philemon 1:20) with the same verb. Ignatius uses it again at 12:1 and in Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:2, 'May I always have the benefit of you'.

a: as to the law of Jesus Christ
p: The overseer is received 'as the grace of God', the elders 'as the law of Jesus Christ'.
b: Ignatius pairs the two offices with two gifts: grace and law. He does not explain the pairing. Paul speaks of 'the law of Christ' (Galatians 6:2). Lightfoot, quoting this verse in The Christian Ministry, sets it among the letters' sayings in which the elders 'are not put out of sight' beside the overseer.

a: You too should not take advantage of your overseer's youth
p: Damas was young, and some may have thought little of him for it.
b: Greek mē synchrasthai tē hēlikia tou episkopou, 'not to take advantage of the age of the overseer'. Lake: 'not to presume on the youth of the bishop'. Paul tells Timothy, 'Let no one treat your youth with contempt' (1 Timothy 4:12). Ignatius's answer is the same as Paul's in kind but different in ground: respect is owed not to the man's years but to God the Father, whom the overseer stands for. The elders, older men, are praised for deferring to him.
orig: μὴ συγχρᾶσθαι τῇ ἡλικίᾳ τοῦ ἐπισκόπου

a: the overseer of all
p: Ignatius plays on the word: the Father is the true overseer behind the visible one.
b: Greek tō pantōn episkopō. The word episkopos ('overseer', the word behind 'bishop') is kept for God too, so the reader sees the play: the elders yield not to the young man but 'to the Father of Jesus Christ, the overseer of all'. 1 Peter 2:25 calls Christ 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls'. 3:2 adds the visible and the unseen overseer. Lightfoot quotes the line in The Christian Ministry among the letters' 'far stronger expressions' for the office.

a: He is cheating the one who cannot be seen
t: The seen and the unseen overseer
p: To deceive the visible overseer is to try to deceive God.
b: Greek ton episkopon touton ton blepomenon ... ton aoraton paralogizetai. Hypocrisy toward the overseer is not a matter of human relations ('his reckoning is not with flesh'), but of dealing with God, 'who knows the hidden things'. The thought is close to Peter's word to Ananias: 'It was not people you lied to. It was God' (Acts 5:4).

a: not only to be called Christians, but to be Christians
t: Christians in name and in fact
p: The name 'Christian' was still new; Ignatius wants the life to match it.
b: Greek Christianous. The disciples were first called 'Christians' at Antioch, Ignatius's own city (Acts 11:26). Lightfoot: in the New Testament the word 'is still more or less a term of reproach; in the age of Ignatius it has become a title of honour'. Ignatius uses it to test a claim: some 'call him overseer, yet they do everything without him'. Jesus says the same of 'Lord, Lord' (Luke 6:46).
orig: μὴ μόνον καλεῖσθαι Χριστιανούς, ἀλλὰ καὶ εἶναι

a: their meetings are not valid or held as commanded
p: The word is the 'valid' of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1.
b: Greek dia to mē bebaiōs kat' entolēn synathroizesthai, 'because they do not gather validly according to command'. Lake: 'since they do not hold valid meetings according to the commandments'. The adverb is from bebaios, 'firm, valid', the word of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1: 'Count that thanksgiving valid which is under the overseer'. Ignatius does not say what the 'command' is. The people he means meet, but apart from the overseer; that, for him, makes the meeting unsound.
orig: διὰ τὸ μὴ βεβαίως κατ᾽ ἐντολὴν συναθροίζεσθαι

a: his own place
p: Lake's margin points to Acts 1:25, where Judas goes 'to his own place'.
b: Greek eis ton idion topon, the words of Acts 1:25: Judas turned aside 'to go to his own place'. Ignatius makes it general: death and life lie before everyone, and each goes where he belongs. The choice of two ways, life and death, is old (Deuteronomy 30:15, 19).

a: It is like two coins
p: Each person carries a stamp, like a coin: the world's or God's.
b: Greek nomismata dyo, each with its own charaktēr, 'stamp'. Lake translates 'two coinages' and notes: 'This is perhaps a reference to Mt. xxii. 19.' There Jesus asks to see 'the coin you pay the tax with' and whose image is on it (Matthew 22:19-20). In Ignatius the stamp the believer bears is God the Father's, given 'in love' and 'through Jesus Christ'. Hebrews 1:3 uses the same word charaktēr of the Son: 'the exact stamp of his being' (Hebrews 1:3).

a: Unless we freely choose to die through him into his suffering
p: Christ's life is in those who choose to share his death.
b: Greek ean mē authairetōs echōmen to apothanein eis to autou pathos. Authairetōs is 'of one's own free choice'. Lake: 'unless we willingly choose to die through him in his passion'. Paul says believers are 'grown together with him in a death like his' (Romans 6:5) and that he wants 'to share his sufferings' (Philippians 3:10). For Ignatius, on his way to the beasts, the words were also literal.
orig: ἐὰν μὴ αὐθαιρέτως ἔχωμεν τὸ ἀποθανεῖν εἰς τὸ αὐτοῦ πάθος

a: with the overseer presiding
t: The overseer 'in the place of God': how it is read
p: Catholic teaching, an Orthodox reference work and the Anglican Lightfoot read this order differently.
b:
Catholic: 'In the beautiful expression of St. Ignatius of Antioch, the bishop is typos tou Patros: he is like the living image of God the Father' (Catechism 1549, citing Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1 and this verse). An Orthodox reference work: The A to Z of the Orthodox Church (Prokurat, Golitzin and Peterson, 2010), a dictionary and not a church's statement, says of the letters as a whole that 'Ignatius stresses the importance of the bishop, the centrality of the Eucharist, and a Christology ... that insists on the reality of the eternal Word come in the flesh'; it does not discuss this verse.

Lightfoot, Anglican scholar and Bishop of Durham: 'If the bishop occupies the place of God or of Jesus Christ, the presbyters are as the Apostles, as the council of God'; he called it an 'extravagant exaltation of the episcopal office', explained by 'the needs and distractions of the age' (The Christian Ministry, pages 87-88).

The churches' own teaching on bishops and elders is on the cards at Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3; succession: 2 Timothy 2.
r: Acts 20:28; Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:1-7; Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1

a: the council of the apostles
t: The elders as the apostles' council
p: The elders sit round the overseer as the apostles sat round Christ.
b: Greek synedrion tōn apostolōn; synedrion is a council (the same word names the Jewish Sanhedrin in the Gospels). Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1 calls the elders 'God's council' and 'the band of apostles'. The picture is of a council seated with its head; Ignatius does not say here that the elders succeed the apostles in office. Lightfoot's word for the elders' place is 'a council ... round the bishop'.

a: entrusted with the ministry of Jesus Christ
p: Lake thinks the sentence about the deacons was left unfinished.
b: Greek pepisteumenōn diakonian Iēsou Christou. The overseer presides 'in the place of God', the elders 'in the place of the council of the apostles', but the deacons get no matching phrase. Lake's English footnote: 'The sentences seem to be unfinished', and he points to a later church order, the Apostolic Constitutions (2.26), which does give one. Lightfoot supplies a word such as 'being present' for the deacons and reads the clause as the reason: 'seeing that they have been entrusted' with Christ's own service (diakonia, the word behind 'deacon').

a: He was with the Father before the ages and appeared at the end
p: A two-line confession: the Son was with the Father before time and appeared at its end.
b: Greek hos pro aiōnōn para patri ēn kai en telei ephanē. John opens with the Word who 'was with God' (John 1:1), and Hebrews says, 'At the end of these days he has spoken to us in a Son' (Hebrews 1:2). Lightfoot cites this line as one place where Ignatius 'asserts the eternity of the Son in the most explicit terms', which bears on how to read 'came forth from silence' at 8:2.
orig: ὃς πρὸ αἰώνων παρὰ πατρὶ ἦν καὶ ἐν τέλει ἐφάνη

a: Let no one look at his neighbor by the flesh
p: Paul too says, 'from now on we know no one by the flesh'.
b: Greek mēdeis kata sarka blepetō ton plēsion. Paul: 'So from now on we know no one by the flesh' (2 Corinthians 5:16). Ignatius means: do not judge one another by human standards (age, rank, appearance, as with the young overseer of 3:1), but love one another in Christ.
orig: μηδεὶς κατὰ σάρκα βλεπέτω τὸν πλησίον

a: as a type and a lesson of incorruption
p: The united church is itself a picture and a lesson of the life that does not decay.
b: Greek eis typon kai didachēn aphtharsias. Typos is a stamp, model or picture (as in 5:2's stamp, and Romans 5:14, 'a figure of the one who was coming'). The Plain English Translation uses 'type' in all three places in this letter and in Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1, so the reader sees the one word. Aphtharsia, 'incorruption', is the life that cannot decay (1 Corinthians 15:42). Lake: 'as an example and lesson of immortality'.

a: did nothing without him
t: The Son does nothing on his own
p: Lake's margin points to John 5:19, 5:30 and 8:28.
b: Jesus says, 'the Son is not able to do anything on his own' (John 5:19), 'I am not able to do a single thing on my own' (John 5:30), and 'I do nothing from myself' (John 8:28). Ignatius draws the lesson for the church: as the Son with the Father, so the church with its overseer and elders. On the margin: one scan of Lake reads 'Joh. 5, 19. 30; 8, 28'.

a: one prayer, one request, one mind, one hope
p: The repeated 'one' of 7:1-2 recalls Ephesians 4:4-6.
b: Greek mia proseuchē, mia deēsis, heis nous, mia elpis, and then 'one temple ... one altar ... one Jesus Christ ... one Father' (7:2). Paul's list is 'one body and one Spirit ... one hope ... One Lord, one faith, one baptism. One God and Father of all' (Ephesians 4:4-6). 'When you meet in one place' is Greek epi to auto, the phrase of Acts 2:1 ('gathered together in the same place') and of Ignatius to the Ephesians 13:1.
orig: μία προσευχή, μία δέησις, εἷς νοῦς, μία ἐλπίς

a: one temple of God, as to one altar
p: Ignatius pictures the gathered church as a temple with one altar.
b: Greek hōs eis hena naon ... hōs epi hen thysiastērion. 'Altar' (thysiastērion) is Ignatius's word for the place where the united church stands: 'If anyone is not within the altar, he goes without God's bread' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2); and in To the Philadelphians 4:1 he joins 'one thanksgiving', 'one cup' and 'one altar' with 'one overseer'. Paul calls the church God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16). Hebrews 13:10 says, 'We have an altar'.
orig: ὡς εἰς ἕνα ναὸν ... ὡς ἐπὶ ἓν θυσιαστήριον
r: 1 Corinthians 3:16; Hebrews 13:10; Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2

a: came forth from the one Father, was with the one, and went back to the one
p: The words follow Jesus's own: 'I came out from the Father ... going on my way to the Father'.
b: Greek ton aph' henos patros proelthonta kai eis hena onta kai chōrēsanta. Jesus says, 'I came out from the Father and have come into the world. Now in turn I am leaving the world and going on my way to the Father' (John 16:28). 'Was with the one' takes up 6:1, 'He was with the Father before the ages'. 'Came forth' is the verb of 8:2, 'his Word, who came forth from silence'.
orig: ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς πατρὸς προελθόντα καὶ εἰς ἕνα ὄντα καὶ χωρήσαντα

a: other opinions
p: Greek heterodoxiai, the family of the later word 'heterodoxy'.
b: Greek heterodoxiai, 'other opinions', from heteros, 'other', and doxa, 'opinion'. The same family stands in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 6:2, 'those who hold other opinions about the grace of Jesus Christ'. Here the other opinions are tied to 'old myths' and to living 'by Judaism'.

a: old myths that are of no use
p: The pastoral letters warn against 'myths' too, and Titus calls them 'Jewish myths'.
b: Greek mytheumasin tois palaiois anōphelesin ousin. 1 Timothy 1:4 warns 'not to pay attention to myths and endless genealogies', and Titus 1:14 speaks of 'Jewish myths'. Titus 3:9 calls such debates things that 'do no good'. Ignatius does not say what the old myths were.

a: if we are still living by Judaism to this day
p: Ignatius uses Paul's word, Ioudaismos, the Jewish way of life.
b: Greek kata Ioudaismon zōmen. Ioudaismos is the word Paul uses of his own past: 'how I used to live when I was in Judaism' (Galatians 1:13-14). Ignatius's claim is that to go on living by it 'to this day', after Christ, is to confess that 'we have not received grace'. The sentence is written to Christians and about a way of life among Christians; who exactly held it is the question of the note at 10:3. Lake's introduction: 'it is disputed whether he means that this was an evil found in docetic circles, or that it was a danger threatening the church from other directions.'

a: the most godly prophets lived by Christ Jesus
p: For Ignatius the prophets were already Christ's people, and were persecuted for it.
b: Greek hoi theiotatoi prophētai kata Christon Iēsoun ezēsan. The prophets 'searched for' the salvation to come, and 'the Spirit of Christ within them' bore witness in advance (1 Peter 1:10-11); Lightfoot notes how closely Ignatius's picture of the prophets resembles Peter's. Jesus says, 'People persecuted the prophets who lived before you in the same way' (Matthew 5:12; Acts 7:52). So the prophets are not on the side of 'Judaism' in Ignatius's sense, but on Christ's (9:2). Lightfoot: for Ignatius the prophets are 'the forerunners of the Gospel', with 'an absolute identity of interests' between them.
orig: οἱ γὰρ θειότατοι προφῆται κατὰ Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν ἔζησαν

a: from silence
p: God was silent; then he spoke his Word. Lightfoot reads it of the incarnation.
b:
Greek hos estin autou logos apo sigēs proelthōn. Lightfoot: sigē ('silence') and logos ('word') 'are correlative terms, logos implying a previous sigē'. He asks whether the coming forth is the Son's eternal begetting or his coming in the flesh, and decides for the second: 'the whole context here relates to the Incarnation', as 'made himself known' and 'the one who sent him' show; he adds that Ignatius 'does not deny the pre-existence of the Word here, though he does not assert it' (and see 6:1).

Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1 speaks the same way of mysteries 'done in God's quiet', and Paul of 'the mystery kept in silence for long ages' (Romans 16:25). John: 'In the beginning was the Word' (John 1:1). On the reading 'not from silence', see the variant.
r: John 1:1; Romans 16:25; Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1; 6:1

a: In every way the Son pleased the one who sent him
t: He pleased the one who sent him
p: Lightfoot hears John 8:29.
b: Greek hos kata panta euērestēsen tō pempsanti auton. Lightfoot: 'A reminiscence of John viii. 29': 'The one who sent me is with me ... at all times I do what he finds pleasing' (John 8:29). The Plain English Translation writes 'the Son' for the Greek 'who', to keep the reader clear on who pleased whom.
orig: ὃς κατὰ πάντα εὐηρέστησεν τῷ πέμψαντι αὐτόν

a: those who lived in the old ways
t: Who came to a new hope?
p: Lightfoot: Jewish converts. Hilgenfeld (as Lightfoot reports him) and Fritz Guy: the prophets.
b:
Greek hoi en palaiois pragmasin anastraphentes, 'those who lived in old practices'. Two readings:

Jewish believers. Lightfoot: 'those who were brought up in the practices of Judaism'. If even Jewish converts gave up keeping Sabbaths, 'a fortiori ought Gentile converts not to barter Christ for Judaic rites'. 'No longer' points to a change, which cannot be said of the prophets.

The prophets. Hilgenfeld, as Lightfoot reports him, referred the words to the prophets after Moses; Lightfoot rejects this. Fritz Guy (1964) also reads the sentence as about 'the divine prophets' of 8:2, and so takes 'no longer keeping the Sabbath' as a picture of leaving a legalistic attitude rather than leaving a day.

The Plain English Translation keeps the Greek's open subject, 'Those who lived in the old ways'.

a: no longer keeping the Sabbath
t: 'No longer keeping the Sabbath': how it is read
p: The most-quoted early line on Sunday and the Sabbath. Its text and its sense are both argued.
b:
Greek mēketi sabbatizontes, alla kata kyriakēn zōntes. Sabbatizō is not in the New Testament but is frequent in the Greek Old Testament, 'where it bears a good sense' (Lightfoot). The line is part of a condition ('If, then, ...'), whose conclusion is the question of 9:2, 'how will we be able to live without him?'. It gives no rule for a day of rest or worship, and has no word for 'day': the brackets mark the word the Plain English Translation supplies, and the one Greek manuscript supplies 'life' instead (see the next note and the variant).

The Catholic Church, in its Catechism, quotes the verse for Sunday, whose 'ceremonial observance replaces that of the sabbath' (Catechism 2175). J. B. Lightfoot, a scholar, not a church: living 'after the Lord's day' means taking on all it stands for, the resurrection. Fritz Guy, a scholar (Andrews University Seminary Studies, 1964): the line 'can not at the present time properly be introduced as evidence' that the Lord's day was kept, nor said with certainty not to allude to it.

The churches' own teaching on the day, Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Baptist and Adventist, is on the card at Revelation 1:10; the card at Colossians 2:16-17 and the Sabbath card at Exodus 20 give more.

a: the Lord's [day]
p: The Greek has the adjective alone: kyriakē, 'the Lord's'.
b: Greek kata kyriakēn, 'by the Lord's', with the noun 'day' left out, as in English one might say 'the Lord's'. Lake translates 'for the Lord's Day', and Lightfoot supplies hēmeran, 'day'. The Plain English Translation supplies 'day' too, in brackets, to show that the word is not in the Greek; the one Greek manuscript has 'life' here instead (see the variant). The full phrase is John's 'It was the Lord's day' (Revelation 1:10, en tē kyriakē hēmera); the Didache has 'On the Lord's day of the Lord' (Didache 14:1). Lightfoot counts this verse, if Revelation 1:10 means the day of judgment as some argued, the earliest use of the word for Sunday, 'except perhaps' the Didache; he notes Melito's book 'On the Lord's Day' and Dionysius of Corinth's 'today we kept the Lord's holy day' (Eusebius, Church History 4.23, as Lightfoot quotes it). The resurrection on 'the first day of the week' (Matthew 28:1; Acts 20:7) is what the name looks back to: 'on which our life also rose'.

a: our only teacher
p: Jesus: 'Your Teacher is one'.
b: Greek tou monou didaskalou hēmōn. Jesus tells his disciples, 'you must not be called "Rabbi." Your Teacher is one, and you are all brothers' (Matthew 23:8). The prophets too looked for him 'as their teacher' (9:2), and so were his disciples (mathētai, 'learners').

a: came and raised them from the dead
p: Lake: probably the belief that Christ went down to the dead and freed the righteous of old.
b: Greek parōn ēgeiren autous ek nekrōn, 'being present, he raised them from the dead'. Lake's footnote: 'This is possibly a proleptic reference to final resurrection, but more probably to the belief, found in many documents of a later date, that Jesus by the descent into Hades set free, and took into Paradise, the righteous dead. Cf. especially the Gospel of Nicodemus or Acta Pilati.' Lake's margin gives Matthew 27:52: 'Tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who slept in death were raised.' Lightfoot adds 1 Peter 3:19 ('he went and made a proclamation to the spirits in prison') and 1 Peter 4:6, and gathers the belief in Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, the Shepherd of Hermas and Clement of Alexandria.

a: Even the prophets were his disciples in the Spirit
p: The prophets learned from Christ by the Spirit before he came.
b: Greek hoi prophētai mathētai ontes tō pneumati. Lightfoot joins 'in the Spirit' to 'looked for him', as 'more consonant with 1 Pet. i. 11': 'the Spirit of Christ within them ... bore witness in advance to the sufferings that would come to Christ' (1 Peter 1:11). Jesus says, 'Abraham your father was overjoyed that he would see my day' (John 8:56).
orig: οἱ προφῆται μαθηταὶ ὄντες τῷ πνεύματι

a: If he were to imitate us in the way we act, we would be finished
p: If God treated us as we treat him, we would be lost.
b: Greek ean gar hēmas mimēsētai katha prassomen, ouketi esmen, 'if he imitates us as we act, we are no more'. Lake's footnote: 'The meaning appears to be "if God should treat us according to human standards none of us should see salvation."' Lightfoot: 'If He were to treat us, as we treat Him, we should indeed be lost.' The psalm asks the same: who could stand if God kept watch over guilt (Psalm 130:3)?
orig: ἐὰν γὰρ ἡμᾶς μιμήσηται καθὰ πράσσομεν, οὐκέτι ἐσμέν

a: let us learn to live by Christianity
p: Lightfoot: Ignatius's letters are the earliest known use of the word.
b: Greek kata Christianismon zēn. Lightfoot: the noun 'Christianity' would have been coined soon after the name 'Christian', 'But these epistles furnish the earliest extant example of its use.' Ignatius sets it against Ioudaismos (8:1; 10:3), and uses it again in Ignatius to the Romans 3:3 and To the Philadelphians 6:1; the Martyrdom of Polycarp 10:1 has it too. To live 'by Christianity' is to live by Christ, as disciples who 'learn' (mathōmen) from him.
r: Ignatius to the Romans 3:3; Martyrdom of Polycarp 10:1; Acts 11:26

a: any name other than this
p: 'This' may be the name Christianity or the name of Christ.
b: Greek allō onomati ... pleon toutou, 'by another name, beyond this'. Lightfoot: '"beyond this," i.e. tou christianismou. Or is it tou onomatos tou Christou?' Either way the point is that the name a believer bears is Christ's. Peter: 'Nowhere under heaven is there another name given among human beings' (Acts 4:12).
orig: ὃς γὰρ ἄλλῳ ὀνόματι καλεῖται πλέον τούτου

a: the bad yeast, which has grown old and sour
p: Lake's margin: 1 Corinthians 5:7. Ignatius makes Christ himself the new yeast.
b: Greek tēn kakēn zymēn, tēn palaiōtheisan kai enoxisasan. Paul: 'Sweep out the old yeast, so that you can be fresh dough, since you are already unleavened bread. For our Passover, Christ, has been slaughtered' (1 Corinthians 5:7), and 'Let us not use old yeast, the yeast of malice and wickedness' (1 Corinthians 5:8). Ignatius changes the picture: the old yeast is what he calls 'Judaism' (10:3), and the new yeast 'is Jesus Christ', as in Jesus's parable the kingdom is like yeast (Matthew 13:33). The site renders zymē 'yeast' in both writers.
orig: τὴν κακὴν ζύμην, τὴν παλαιωθεῖσαν καὶ ἐνοξίσασαν

a: Be salted in him
t: Salted, so as not to go bad
p: Salt keeps food from spoiling; Lightfoot hears the Gospel sayings on salt.
b: Greek halisthēte en autō. Lightfoot: 'Here again is an allusion to another metaphor in the Gospel parables' (Matthew 5:13; Mark 9:50; Luke 14:34), with 'a possible reference' to the law that every grain offering is seasoned with salt (Leviticus 2:13). The picture runs on: salt keeps food from rotting ('so that none of you goes bad'), and bad meat is known by its smell. Ignatius to the Ephesians 17:1 speaks of 'the foul smell of the teaching of the ruler of this age'.
r: Matthew 5:13; Mark 9:50; Luke 14:34; Leviticus 2:13; Ignatius to the Ephesians 17:1

a: It is out of place
p: Greek atopon: literally 'out of place', so strange, absurd. Lake: 'monstrous'.
b: Greek atopon estin, from a-, 'not', and topos, 'place'. Lake and Lightfoot both translate 'monstrous'. The Plain English Translation keeps the plainer sense of the word, 'out of place', since Ignatius's point is that the two things do not belong together.

a: live in the Jewish way
p: The verb is the one Paul uses to Peter at Antioch.
b: Greek ioudaizein, the verb of Galatians 2:14: 'how can you compel the Gentiles to live in the Jewish way?' Paul's question at Antioch was about Gentile believers being pressed to keep the law. Ignatius, the overseer of Antioch, uses the word for Christians who 'talk of Jesus Christ' and still keep to Jewish practice. It describes a practice among Christians; it is not a word about the Jewish people.

a: Christianity did not put its faith in Judaism
p: Lake, Lightfoot and Fritz Guy read the 'Judaism' of these chapters differently.
b:
Ignatius calls the teaching 'Judaism' and 'old myths' (8:1), 'the bad yeast' (10:2), and links it with those who deny Christ's death (9:1) and need to be told of his birth, suffering and resurrection 'truly and surely' (11:1). The letter does not name the teachers, and Ignatius says he does not know that any Magnesians are 'like this' (11:1).

Lake, in his introduction: Ignatius 'protests against any tendency to Judaistic practices, but it is disputed whether he means that this was an evil found in docetic circles, or that it was a danger threatening the church from other directions.' Lightfoot takes the first view: since Ignatius stresses the reality of Christ's birth, passion and resurrection with 'these same teachers in view', 'The heresy therefore is a Docetic Judaism'; in his introduction to To the Trallians he says the same teachers were 'Judaizers also'. Fritz Guy (1964) reads 'Judaizing' here as 'not a matter of external ritual, but an inner, spiritual attitude', legalism, which the prophets themselves left behind.

Lightfoot reads 'every tongue' with Isaiah 66:18: Christianity was 'a larger and better dispensation than Judaism' because it gathered all nations. That is his judgment. The letter's argument is aimed at Christians, and the site's topic Christian Anti-Judaism and the Bible sets out how such lines were later turned against Jews.

a: every tongue that believed in God
p: Lake's margin: Isaiah 66:18, God's promise to gather all nations and tongues.
b: Greek pasa glōssa pisteusasa eis theon synēchthē. In the Greek Isaiah 66:18 God comes 'to gather all the nations and the tongues' (synagagein panta ta ethnē kai tas glōssas, Swete); the site's Isaiah 66:18, from the Hebrew, reads 'to gather all nations and languages'. Ignatius uses the same verb, 'gather'. Compare also 'and every tongue confess' (Philippians 2:11).
orig: πᾶσα γλῶσσα πιστεύσασα εἰς θεὸν συνήχθη

a: not because I know that any of you are like this
p: Ignatius clears the Magnesians: he writes to guard them in advance.
b: Greek ouk epei egnōn tinas ex hymōn houtōs echontas. Lightfoot: 'He acquits the Magnesians of any complicity therein as yet; but, while this false doctrine is abroad, he feels that the warning is not superfluous.' Ignatius to the Trallians 8:1 says the same: 'not that I know of anything of this kind among you'. 'As one less than you' is his usual humility (Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:2, 'the last of the faithful there').
orig: οὐκ ἐπεὶ ἔγνων τινὰς ἐξ ὑμῶν οὕτως ἔχοντας

a: in the time when Pontius Pilate was governor
p: Pilate's name dates the saving events, as later in the creeds.
b: Greek en kairō tēs hēgemonias Pontiou Pilatou, 'in the time of the governorship of Pontius Pilate'. Naming the governor ties the birth, suffering and resurrection to a date in public history, against those who said they only seemed to happen. Ignatius names Pilate again in Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1 and Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:2; 1 Timothy 6:13 speaks of Christ's 'good confession in front of Pontius Pilate'. The creeds later keep his name.
orig: ἐν καιρῷ τῆς ἡγεμονίας Ποντίου Πιλάτου
r: 1 Timothy 6:13; Luke 3:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:2

a: truly and surely
p: Against those who said Christ only seemed to suffer, Ignatius insists: truly.
b: Greek alēthōs kai bebaiōs. 'Truly' is Ignatius's word against the teaching later called docetism, that Christ only seemed to be human and to suffer; it runs four times through Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1-2 and five times through Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1-2. Bebaiōs, 'surely', is the word behind 'valid' in 4:1. Lightfoot reads 'some deny' in 9:1 as the same teaching.

a: I am not equal to one of you who are free
p: Chains do not make Ignatius greater than the free Magnesians.
b: Greek pros hena tōn lelymenōn hymōn ouk eimi, 'I am not (to be set) beside one of you who have been released'. Lake: 'I am not to be compared to one of you that have been set free'. 'Set free' may mean simply not in chains, or set free by Christ (John 8:36); Ignatius does not say. His humility runs through the letters: Ignatius to the Romans 4:3, 'They were free; up to now I am a slave'.
orig: πρὸς ἕνα τῶν λελυμένων ὑμῶν οὐκ εἰμί

a: A righteous person is his own accuser
t: 'As it is written': Proverbs 18:17 in Greek
p: Ignatius quotes the Greek Proverbs, which differs from the Hebrew the site's Proverbs follows.
b:
Greek hōs gegraptai, hoti ho dikaios heautou katēgoros. Lake's margin gives Proverbs 18:17. The Greek Old Testament (Swete) reads dikaios heautou katēgoros en prōtologia, 'a righteous man is his own accuser in his opening speech'. Ignatius quotes its first words, with 'as it is written', the formula for Scripture.

The site's Proverbs 18:17, made from the Hebrew, reads differently: 'In his dispute, the man who goes first seems in the right; then his neighbor shows up and puts him to the test.' So the Plain English Translation here follows Ignatius's Greek, not the site's Proverbs. Ignatius applies it to the Magnesians' modesty: when praised, they blush. Lightfoot notes that the only formal quotations in the seven letters are from the Old Testament (Proverbs 3:34 in Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:3; this verse; Isaiah 52:5 in Ignatius to the Trallians 8:2).
orig: ὡς γέγραπται, ὅτι ὁ δίκαιος ἑαυτοῦ κατήγορος
r: Proverbs 18:17; Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:3; Ignatius to the Trallians 8:2

a: the decrees of the Lord and of the apostles
p: Greek dogmata, the word for the Jerusalem council's 'decrees' in Acts 16:4.
b: Greek tois dogmasin tou kyriou kai tōn apostolōn. Acts 16:4 uses the word of 'the decrees decided by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem'. Ignatius does not list the decrees; he joins the Lord's teaching and the apostles' as one standard to be 'made firm' in. Ignatius to the Trallians 7:1 speaks likewise of 'the ordinances of the apostles'. How Scripture and tradition relate is the card at 2 Thessalonians 2:15.
orig: ἐν τοῖς δόγμασιν τοῦ κυρίου καὶ τῶν ἀποστόλων
r: Acts 16:4; 2 Thessalonians 2:15; Ignatius to the Trallians 7:1

a: everything you do may turn out well for you
p: Lake's margin and Lake's English point to Psalm 1:3.
b: Greek panta, hosa poieite, kateuodōthēte. The Greek Psalm 1:3 ends panta hosa an poiē kateuodōthēsetai, 'all that he does will prosper' (Swete): the same words, turned to 'you'. Lake prints them in quotation marks. The site's Psalm 1:3, from the Hebrew, says, 'All that he does turns out well'; the Plain English Translation uses its wording, since the Hebrew and the Greek agree here.

a: in the Son and the Father and in the Spirit
p: A threefold name, with the Son named first.
b: Greek en huiō kai patri kai en pneumati. The three are named together as in Matthew 28:19 ('the Father and ... the Son and ... the Holy Spirit'), but the Son comes first, as in Paul's blessing, 'The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit' (2 Corinthians 13:14). 13:2 names the three again in two witnesses (see the variants).
orig: ἐν υἱῷ καὶ πατρὶ καὶ ἐν πνεύματι

a: that well-woven spiritual crown
p: The elders around the overseer are a woven wreath.
b: Greek axioplokou pneumatikou stephanou tou presbyteriou, 'the worthily woven spiritual crown, your council of elders'. A stephanos is a wreath, the kind given to winners in the games (1 Corinthians 9:25). Lightfoot, in The Christian Ministry, quotes the phrase among the lines that keep the elders in sight beside the overseer: 'They form a council, a "worthy spiritual coronal" round the bishop'. Ignatius to the Ephesians 4:1 has another picture: the elders fitted to the overseer 'as strings are to a lyre'.

a: Be subject to the overseer and to one another
p: Submission runs both ways: to the overseer, and to one another.
b: Greek hypotagēte tō episkopō kai allēlois. Paul: 'submitting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ' (Ephesians 5:21). Ignatius grounds it in the Son's own subjection to the Father, as in 1 Corinthians 15:28: 'the Son himself will also be put under the One who put all things under him'. He does not say the Son is less than the Father; elsewhere he calls him 'our God' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2).
r: Ephesians 5:21; 1 Corinthians 15:28; Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2

a: the church in Syria
p: Ignatius's own church, at Antioch, which he asks every church to pray for.
b: The church in Syria is the church at Antioch, which Ignatius led (Ignatius to the Romans 2:2, 'the overseer of Syria'). Every letter from Smyrna asks for prayer for it. From Troas he writes that it is now at peace, and asks the churches to send envoys to rejoice with it (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:1-2). 'I am not worthy to be called one of its people' is his usual humility (Ignatius to the Trallians 13:1).
r: Ignatius to the Romans 9:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:1-2; Ignatius to the Trallians 13:1

a: refreshed with dew
p: In a dry land dew is life; the Magnesians' prayer is to be dew for Antioch.
b: Greek drosisthēnai, 'to be bedewed'. Lake: 'that the Church which is in Syria may be granted refreshment from the dew of your Church'. God says, 'To Israel I will be like the dew' (Hosea 14:5), and the psalm likens unity among brothers to 'Hermon's dew' (Psalm 133:3).

a: The Ephesians greet you from Smyrna
p: The Ephesians' delegates were with Ignatius at Smyrna when he wrote.
b: Ignatius writes from Smyrna, where Ephesus too had sent delegates (Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:1, 'those you sent to Smyrna'). Eusebius, followed by Lake, says that from Smyrna Ignatius wrote to Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles and Rome (Church History 3.36.5). Lightfoot notes that Ephesus and Magnesia were near neighbors, which explains why they appear together here. Who 'refreshed' him is read two ways. Lake's English, followed here, makes it the Ephesians, 'together with Polycarp'. Lightfoot reads 'as you are too' as the Magnesians present through their delegates (2:1), and takes 'together with Polycarp' 'perhaps better' with 'greet you', comparing Ignatius to the Trallians 13:1; the long recension reads 'you refreshed me' (see the variant).
r: Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 12:1

a: Polycarp, overseer of the Smyrnaeans
p: The overseer of Smyrna, Ignatius's host, later martyred himself.
b: Polycarp, the overseer of Smyrna, was with Ignatius there. Ignatius later wrote to him from Troas (To Polycarp), and Polycarp in turn collected Ignatius's letters for the church at Philippi: 'we have sent you the letters of Ignatius, the ones he sent us, and the others we had here with us' (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2). His own death at Smyrna is told in the Martyrdom of Polycarp.
r: Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2; Martyrdom of Polycarp 9:3

a: an unwavering spirit, which is Jesus Christ
p: Greek adiakritos: unwavering, or undivided. Lake hesitates between the two.
b: Greek adiakriton pneuma, hos estin Iēsous Christos. Lake translates 'an unhesitating spirit' and adds: 'The translation "a spirit that knows no division" is possible, and perhaps suits the context here better', pointing to Ignatius to the Trallians 1:1. Lightfoot: 'unwavering, steadfast'. 'Which is Jesus Christ' is, in Lightfoot's view, said of the whole wish for concord: unity is Christ himself, as in Ignatius to the Trallians 11:2, 'God promises union, which is himself'.
orig: ἀδιάκριτον πνεῦμα, ὅς ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς Χριστός
r: Ignatius to the Trallians 1:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 11:2; James 1:6
